chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
title: The Houston battle against Milton Larkin, promoted by Don Robey
summary: Don Robey invites Fields to Houston to play beside Milton Larkin's band with Cobb and Jacquet; Fields mentions Fred Beckett and wanting Tadd Dameron to arrange.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: they went on before. They were later. And I'll tell you the truth, you see when they begin to talk about my band, as Hal Singer said, he loved me, he says I got him where he could be seen. Don Robert (phonetic spelling) said it meant so much in developing musicians, you know, that promoter in Houston, well I played Denison, Texas and that was his home at one time, he happened to be in Denison on some business--

Yeah, but he was in Houston then and happened to be in Denison and he happened to catch the group. He says you must come to Houston, you must come to Houston and bring the band. So we set up a date and got together and went to Houston and it was well worth it, but to show you--I'm trying to think what year it was--but he was only guaranteeing me a hundred and twenty five dollars a night, and I was going clear to Houston, but we had some percentage figured in there, but it finally

worked out to be real good, because he had me booked besides Milton Larkin and that was when Arnett Cobb and Jacquett was in the band, and of course he had heard about--I don't know if I had Bud Douglass yes--but anyway, before I had--I was standing tenor man--well everybody (inaudible) Luther West and Spurgeons and of course (inaudible). He said you sure have a fine sax man.
But when we went to Houston, it wasn't billed like the deal in Denver at that time.
It was still like a battle of the bands?
That's when Irvin and Arnett Cobb and Milton Larkin were in there.
Yeah, Fred Beckett was trombone; and I'm trying to think of his fine piano player; he was a fine arranger*.
I tried a long time to get him in
the band, a very fine arranger. That's when I would go to Rene and say, you see how those arrangements are? They are good and it's not a lot of notes.
Basie's band was known for that, an economy of notes, swing and efficient.
